scoring.formula: raw[axis] = sum(mult * effect[axis]); max[axis] = sum(abs(effect[axis])); score[axis] = 100 * (max + raw) / (2 * max)

meta.presentation: Stored grouped by axis for maintainability. The app must SHUFFLE at runtime with a fixed seed so consecutive items do not come from the same axis.

questions.text: The monarch should hold real, personal decision-making power, not merely a ceremonial role.
Ultimate sovereignty properly rests in the person of the monarch, not in a legislature.
A crown without real governing power has lost the thing that makes monarchy worthwhile.
The monarch's personal judgment should be able to override the counsel of ministers when necessary.
Executive authority concentrated in the monarch is more decisive and coherent than authority spread across institutions.
The crown's power should not be reduced to signing what parliament has already decided.
The monarch should reign but not rule, with real governing power resting in elected or constitutional bodies.
A ceremonial monarchy, above ordinary politics, does more for national unity than one that governs directly.
Political power exercised through accountable institutions is preferable to power concentrated in one person, even a monarch.
The crown's value lies in continuity and symbolism, not in exercising personal command.
Constitutional limits on the monarch protect the institution as much as they protect the people.
A monarch confined to ceremonial duties is fulfilling, not diminishing, the office's proper role.
Legitimate rule passes by hereditary right and divine sanction, not by popular consent.
A monarch's claim to the throne rests on bloodline, not on the approval of the governed.
The legitimacy of a dynasty does not depend on whether the current generation performs well.
Succession by blood provides a stability and continuity that no elected office can match.
God-given right, not the people's will, is the true foundation of royal authority.
A rightful heir's claim stands regardless of how popular or unpopular they personally are.
A ruler's legitimacy ultimately depends on the consent and acclaim of the people they govern.
Effective, popular leadership is a more solid basis for authority than inherited bloodline.
A ruler who has lost the people's confidence has lost their legitimacy, whatever their lineage.
Authority earned through demonstrated capability outranks authority claimed through birth.
A social or constitutional contract, not divine right, is what properly grounds a ruler's power.
Even a monarch's legitimacy ultimately rests on some form of public acceptance.
The state should be formally bound to a single confessional church and its teachings.
The monarch's authority is properly understood as sanctioned and blessed by the church.
Church and throne should stand together as mutually reinforcing pillars of the social order.
Religious orthodoxy should be actively defended and enforced by the crown.
The nation's laws should reflect and be answerable to the teachings of its established church.
A monarchy without a religious foundation lacks the deeper legitimacy that sustains it.
The state's authority should rest on secular, civil grounds, independent of any church's blessing.
Religious and political authority should be kept separate, even under a monarchy.
A monarch's legitimacy shouldn't depend on the endorsement of any religious institution.
Erastian control of the church by the state is preferable to the church holding independent authority.
The crown should treat religious institutions as subordinate to civil authority, not as a co-equal pillar of order.
A modern monarchy is stronger when it isn't bound to any one confessional tradition.
Society is naturally and rightly ordered into estates and ranks, each with its own duties and privileges.
Formal social hierarchy, recognised in law, reflects a natural and legitimate order.
Different classes of society properly have different rights, obligations, and legal standing.
A hereditary nobility with its own privileges is a legitimate and stabilising feature of society.
Corporate bodies — guilds, estates, orders — properly mediate between the individual and the crown.
Formal legal distinctions between ranks of society preserve a natural and functional order.
All subjects should be equal before the law, regardless of birth or rank.
Legal privilege attached to noble birth has no place in a well-ordered modern state.
A single, uniform citizenship is a fairer basis for society than a hierarchy of legal estates.
Formal distinctions of rank in law should give way to equal legal status for all.
The abolition of legal privilege by birth was a genuine improvement, not a loss, in social order.
A modern monarchy is more legitimate when all its subjects share the same legal standing.
Historic regional rights, charters, and local privileges deserve to be respected and preserved.
A kingdom made up of distinct provinces with their own traditional laws is a legitimate model of order.
Local and regional autonomy should be protected against absorption into a single centralised administration.
Traditional local liberties are worth defending even against the crown's own centralising instincts.
A patchwork of regional laws and customs reflects the organic, historical character of the realm.
Centralising every function of government erodes the local attachments that give a kingdom its cohesion.
A single, unified legal and administrative system across the whole realm is the mark of a well-ordered state.
Regional privileges and local exceptions weaken the crown's ability to govern effectively.
The crown should override local particularism in favour of uniform, centrally administered law.
A strong, centralised monarchy is more capable of defending the realm than one fragmented by local privilege.
Absolute royal authority is best exercised through a single, unified administration, not through regional intermediaries.
Uniform centralisation, even at the cost of local tradition, serves the strength of the state.
The traditional agrarian order — land, estate, and peasant obligation — is the proper economic foundation of the realm.
Guild and corporate regulation of trade and craft is preferable to unregulated commerce.
Land tied to noble estates and inherited obligation is a more stable economic basis than commercial exchange.
Rapid commercial and industrial change threatens the social bonds a traditional economy depends on.
The economy should serve the traditional social order, not reshape it in the name of efficiency.
Restraining commercial and financial interests protects the older, more stable agrarian foundation of society.
A modern commercial and capitalist economy is compatible with, and can strengthen, monarchical rule.
The crown should encourage trade, industry, and commercial growth rather than defend an agrarian order against them.
Economic modernisation, even where it disrupts old estates and guilds, ultimately strengthens the realm.
A monarchy that embraces commerce and enterprise is more durable than one tied to an agrarian past.
Financial and mercantile interests can be valuable allies of the crown, not threats to it.
The traditional agrarian economy is not worth preserving at the cost of the realm's commercial strength.
Restoration of the monarchy should proceed through legal, constitutional, and peaceful means.
Patient legal and diplomatic effort is the proper route to restoring rightful rule.
A restoration achieved through negotiation and legitimate process carries more lasting authority than one imposed by force.
Working within existing legal and political structures is the responsible path back to monarchy.
A monarchist movement should renounce violence and pursue restoration by lawful means.
Gradual, institutional change is more likely to produce a durable restoration than any sudden seizure of power.
Restoration may legitimately require an uprising, coup, or armed struggle if legal channels are closed.
Waiting on legal process when the crown has been unjustly displaced can mean waiting forever.
A rightful monarch's cause justifies the use of force to reclaim the throne when necessary.
History shows that restorations have usually come through decisive action, not patient legalism.
A monarchist movement that rules out force in principle has no real path back to power.
Direct action to restore the crown is legitimate when the existing order has no lawful path to change.
Monarchist politics is properly the business of the aristocracy, the court, and established elites.
Restoration should be pursued through influence over elites and institutions, not popular mobilisation.
A monarchist movement should be cautious about appeals to the masses, which can spiral beyond its control.
The legitimacy of monarchy rests on tradition and elite continuity, not on popular enthusiasm.
Popular political mobilisation is a poor fit for a cause grounded in inherited, not democratic, legitimacy.
Court and aristocratic politics, not mass rallies, are the proper terrain for a monarchist movement.
A monarchist cause needs to build genuine popular support to have any chance of succeeding today.
Mass mobilisation and popular appeal are necessary tools for restoring a monarchy in the modern era.
A restored monarchy needs the demonstrated backing of ordinary people, not just elite favour, to be secure.
Popular plebiscite or acclaim can be a legitimate part of restoring a monarch to power.
A monarchist movement should actively organise and appeal to popular sentiment, not rely on elite networks alone.
Winning over the crowd is as important to a modern restoration as winning over the aristocracy.
